title: Data, features & labels
intro: The language of ML data: rows are samples, columns are features, and the column you predict is the target. What X and y look like in scikit-learn, which kinds of features exist — and why splitting into train and test is non-negotiable.

sections.title: Thinking in tables: rows and columns

blocks.html: Almost every ML dataset starts as a table. Each row is one sample (also called: observation or instance) — one car, one person, one email. Each column is a variable describing that sample. Machine learning comes down to finding patterns between those columns.

As an example we take the car dataset that also returns in the Evaluation & metrics chapter: five cars, each described by three characteristics, with the price as the thing we want to predict. The table is deliberately small: 5 rows, 4 columns.

Jargon check: feature = input column (also: independent variable, explanatory variable). Target / label = the column you predict (dependent variable). In mathematical texts the target is also called y and the features x.

sections.title: X and y: the scikit-learn convention

blocks.html: scikit-learn always expects data in two parts: X, the feature matrix (capital letter, because it is two-dimensional), and y, the target vector (lower case, because it is one-dimensional). Each row of X corresponds exactly to one element of y — row 3 of X describes the same car as element 3 of y.

blocks.label: shape of the data
blocks.caption: n = number of samples (rows), p = number of features (columns). The model learns the mapping from each row x_i to a prediction y-hat.

blocks.html: Below you see how to turn the car table into X and y with numpy — and how to read out the shapes and the first pair. This pattern (preparing data, checking shapes) is always your first step in scikit-learn.

blocks.caption: the car table as X and y
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

# rows = cars, columns = [age, mileage, owners]
X = np.array([[1,  5, 1],
              [3, 12, 2],
              [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3],
              [9, 30, 2]], dtype=float)

y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4])   # price (x1000 EUR)

print('X has shape:', X.shape, '-> n = 5 samples, p = 3 features')
print('y has shape:', y.shape, '-> 1 target per sample')
print('features of car 1:', X[0], '-> price:', y[0])

sections.title: Kinds of features (and how to prepare them)

blocks.html: Features come in three flavours. Numerical features are numbers mathematics may operate on (age, mileage). Categorical features are labels: nominal (red/blue — no order) or ordinal (low/medium/high — with order). Models compute with numbers, so categorical features must be encoded: nominal via one-hot (one column per category), ordinal may become 0/1/2.

rows: larger scales dominate distance-based models → scale/standardise
one-hot encoding; never 1/2/3 — that suggests an order that is not there
may be 0/1/2, because the order is meaningful

blocks.html: Garbage in, garbage out. A model is never better than its features: missing values, outliers and wrongly encoded categories lead directly to a bad model. Exploring and cleaning data is not a side note — it is often most of the work of the whole project.

sections.title: Train and test: evaluate on unseen data

blocks.html: The golden rule: never evaluate on the data you trained on. A model that memorises the training data scores perfectly there and fails in the real world. Just like an exam: you saw the answers of old exams while practising, not those of the real exam. That is why you split the data: a large part to train on (often 75–80%) and a smaller part to test honestly.
Below the complete mini-flow: split, train a simple model, and print both scores. Note the difference — the train score is almost always higher, and it is the test score that counts.

blocks.caption: train/test split with KNN
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

X = np.array([[1,  5, 1], [3, 12, 2], [4, 15, 1],
              [7, 23, 3], [9, 30, 2], [2,  9, 1],
              [6, 20, 3], [8, 26, 2]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([18, 12, 10, 6, 4, 15, 8, 5], dtype=float)

# 75% train, 25% test — the model NEVER sees the test rows
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

model = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=3).fit(X_train, y_train)
print('train score (optimistic):', model.score(X_train, y_train).round(2))
print('test score  (honest)    :', model.score(X_test, y_test).round(2))

new_car = [[5, 17, 1]]
print('predicted price (x1000 EUR):', model.predict(new_car)[0].round(1))

blocks.html: The train score is an optimistic diagnosis, the test score the honest one. Only the test score says something about how the model will do in the real world. The next topic shows how this protects against under- and overfitting.
